endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: The applicability of suggested actions to relevant AI actors should be determined based on organizational considerations and their unique uses of GAI systems.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: High-risk AI solutions should be visible within existing risk registers and, where appropriate, escalated to executive or board-level oversight consistent with the organization's risk governance model.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: GV.RM-P2: Organizational risk tolerance is determined and clearly expressed.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: If any risk is judged unacceptable, it should be reduced to 698 acceptable levels by the appropriate means.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: The opportunity for a patient or their caregiver to request additional review from a licensed clinician should be made available upon request.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether defining AI risk tolerance, holding deployments within it, and signing time-bound residual risk acceptance reduce unacknowledged exposure to AI risk. Five frameworks and guidance documents endorse parts of the practice, so support for it currently rests on expert consensus rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so no certainty rating can be assigned under GRADE conventions. The five endorsements are consensus statements. They can indicate agreement among bodies, but they do not estimate whether the practice changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes.

The endorsements emphasize different elements. The CHAI guide asks that risk tolerance be determined and expressed, and the CHAI playbooks ask that high-risk AI appear in risk registers with escalation to executives or the board. The FDA draft guidance asks that unacceptable risk be reduced to acceptable levels. None of the quoted passages addresses the time-bound sign-off element.

The AMA principle quoted here concerns a patient's option to request review by a licensed clinician. It does not speak to enterprise risk tolerance, so it offers indirect support at most. No supplied evidence shows whether board-level risk acceptance affects patients' safety, trust, or access to a human.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without formally defined AI risk tolerance and expiring residual risk sign-offs. Useful outcomes include the number of deployments paused or withdrawn, the time taken to re-review expired acceptances, and AI-related safety events. Descriptive studies that document how often AI risk is accepted without formal acknowledgment would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Governance bodies have no data on whether a risk tolerance set at the enterprise level accounts for risks that fall unevenly on these groups.
